title: UTF-8 to UTF-16 by hand
description:
Write `toUtf16(utf8)`, which converts UTF-8 text into UTF-16 units, the job `MultiByteToWideChar` does. Use `std::u16string` so the code works on any platform.

Decode each character from its UTF-8 bytes (1 to 4 of them, using the table in the lesson) into a code point, then encode the code point as UTF-16:

- code points up to U+FFFF become one unit;
- code points from U+10000 to U+10FFFF become a surrogate pair: subtract 0x10000, then the high unit is `0xD800 + (value >> 10)` and the low unit `0xDC00 + (value & 0x3FF)`.

If the input is not valid UTF-8 (a byte that cannot start a character, a sequence cut short, or a continuation byte that does not start with the bits `10`), return `std::nullopt`.
hints: `std::u16string` works just like `std::string`, except that each element is a `char16_t`, one 16-bit UTF-16 unit. Add a unit with `out.push_back(static_cast<char16_t>(unit));`.

`std::optional<T>` (from `<optional>`) holds either a `T` or nothing. `return value;` gives back a filled one and `return std::nullopt;` an empty one. A caller tests it with `if (result)` (or `result.has_value()`) and reads the value inside with `*result`.

The lead byte's top bits tell you how many continuation bytes follow and which of its own bits belong to the code point: `0xxxxxxx` (0 more, 7 bits), `110xxxxx` (1 more, 5 bits), `1110xxxx` (2 more, 4 bits), `11110xxx` (3 more, 3 bits).

Before reading the continuation bytes, check there are enough bytes left: `i + extra` must be less than `utf8.size()`. Each continuation byte must match `10xxxxxx` (`(byte & 0xC0) == 0x80`) and adds its low 6 bits: `cp = (cp << 6) | (byte & 0x3F)`.
Cast each `char` to `unsigned char` before testing its bits: `char` is signed on Windows, so `0xC3` would otherwise be a negative number.
lessonTitle: Strings on Windows: ANSI, UTF-16 and UTF-8
